theme: Cleansing rituals; bodily discharges, wholeness restored
readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 14:1-15:33. Yesterday ended with the isolation of the unclean person. Today you read the ritual that welcomes a healed person back into the community. As you read, notice how much happens before the person is restored.
settingTheScene: Chapter 13 described how the priest examines someone with a skin disease. Chapter 14 describes what happens when the person is healed. The priest goes out to the person, who is outside the camp, and examines him. If he is healed, a ritual with two birds and a series of offerings brings him back. Chapter 15 describes bodily discharges and the rules for cleansing. These chapters are about restoration. Where chapters 11 to 13 describe the problem, chapters 14 and 15 describe the way back.
observation: The priest “shall go out of the camp” to examine the healed person (14:3).
Two live birds are taken. One is killed over fresh water, and the other, dipped in the blood, is released into the open field (14:4-7).
The person washes, shaves, and bathes, and then may enter the camp, but must stay outside his tent for seven days (14:8-9).
On the eighth day he brings a guilt offering, a sin offering, a burnt offering, and a grain offering (14:10-20).
Blood and oil are put on his right ear, right thumb, and right big toe, as with the priests (14:14, 17).
Provision is made for the poor, who may bring birds in place of lambs (14:21-32).
Chapter 15 describes unclean discharges, and what a person must do to be cleansed: wash, wait, and offer a sacrifice (15:1-30).

The purpose is stated: “Thus you shall keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, so that they may not die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst” (15:31).
interpretation:
The ritual for cleansing is more elaborate than you might expect, and it contains a beautiful picture. The healed person is outside the camp, and the priest comes to him. The priest does not wait at the sanctuary. He goes out to the one who is unclean. It is a small detail with a large meaning.

The two birds are a picture of death and release. One bird is killed, and the other is dipped in its blood and let go. The bird flies away alive and free, covered in the blood of the one that died. This is a picture of substitution and freedom. The death of one gives life to the other.

The anointing of the healed person’s ear, thumb, and toe is the same as in the ordination of the priests (Exodus 29:20). He is restored not only to the community but to something like priestly dignity. A person who was cast out of the camp is brought into the tabernacle courts, marked with blood and oil. The healed leper is treated almost as if he were a priest.

The eight days also repeat the pattern of ordination. A person who has been cleansed is given a new beginning. And the provision for the poor shows again that the way back is open to everyone. No one is permanently excluded because he cannot afford the offering.

Chapter 15 on discharges might seem the most embarrassing material in the Bible, but notice its tone. It treats the body matter-of-factly. Uncleanness is not shameful. It is something that happens in a mortal body, and it has a procedure. The principle in verse 31 is the key. The danger is not the condition itself. It is defiling the tabernacle where God lives. These rules protect the nearness of God.
connection: The Gospels record that Jesus healed lepers and then told them to go and show themselves to the priest (Luke 5:12-14; 17:14). They are fulfilling these chapters. Jesus went outside the camp to reach the unclean, just as the priest did. Hebrews 9:13-14 says, “If the blood of goats and bulls… sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ… purify our conscience.” Paul says that we are “washed” and “sanctified” in the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:11).
application:
Think about the picture of the priest going out of the camp. Thank Jesus for coming to find you when you were far from God.

If you know someone who feels excluded, pray for a way to welcome them.

Recall the moment you were brought into God’s family. Give thanks for the new beginning he gave you.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for coming outside the camp to find you.
Ask him to help you welcome others as he welcomed you.
Tell him what it cost him to bring you home.
